# Methods and how to read this report {.unnumbered}

This chapter defines the terms and conventions used throughout, and states plainly what this report is and is not.

## The pipeline

Evidence moved through four stages: title-and-abstract screening, full-text retrieval, full-text screening, and structured data extraction into an approximately 220-field schema in which each value is tied to a verbatim quote from the source. Following the Cochrane rapid-review approach, screening used a single human reviewer augmented by a calibrated large-language-model second screener, with senior adjudication of disagreements; the model was validated against a human gold-standard set before live use. Extraction likewise paired a single human reviewer with a language model prompted with the segmented full text.

## The status of the numbers in this report — read first

Under the protocol, every quantitative value used in synthesis is to be verified 100% against the source document by a human before it is relied upon. **That verification step has not yet been applied to the values in this report.** Everything here (counts, medians, percentages, directions, quality bands) is machine-extracted and **not yet human-verified**. The report is therefore a characterisation of the evidence base and of the review's *provisional* confidence in each design question, not a set of verified findings. It should be used to see the shape of the evidence and to direct where verification and Phase 5 testing are most needed, and every figure should be read as provisional. This caveat is stated once, here, and signalled briefly in each answer box rather than repeated in full throughout.

## How each question is assessed

**Direction of effect and the vote-count rule.** For the intervention questions, each record's reported direction of effect is coded as favouring the intervention, null, favouring the control, or unclear, and displayed as a harvest plot (Ogilvie et al. 2008) — counts by direction, never pooled. Following the protocol (section 4.5.1) the harvest is also stratified by geographic focus — sub-Saharan Africa, other low- and middle-income, high- and upper-middle-income, and mixed settings — so the reader can see whether the direction holds in the settings that matter for the ULCM and not only in the high-income records that supply most of the volume. The protocol also specifies stratifying by evidence stream; that is *not* reproduced here because the stream field is degenerate in the extraction (almost every record carries the same value), and a split on it would be misleading. The protocol's pre-specified consistency rule is then applied: **at least 75%** of records favouring the intervention is *consistent*; 50–74% is *mixed*; below 50% is *inconsistent*.

**Effect magnitude — a distribution, not a pooled estimate.** Effects are never pooled. For the three questions the protocol singles out for effect-size tabulation — minimum dose (RQ7), active ingredients (RQ5) and group size (RQ10), per section 4.5.2 — the report adds a *forest without pooling*: the standardized effects (SMD, Hedges *g* and Cohen *d* only) are placed on a common scale by orienting each to favour the intervention, that is, taking the reported magnitude and setting its sign from the record's coded direction of effect, because the raw values use inconsistent sign conventions. Implausible values (an absolute effect above 3, almost always an extraction error) are dropped, and the resulting distribution is shown as individual points with its median and interquartile range. This is a description of the spread of reported effects, not a meta-analytic estimate: the points are mostly review-level pooled effects rather than independent trials, the signs are reconstructed from the coded direction rather than read from the value, and the values are unverified. For every other question, and for magnitude in general, direction is taken from the harvest, not from the sign or size of any pooled statistic.

**What the vote-count can and cannot bear — read this before the percentages.** Two features of this method must be kept in view throughout, because they weaken every "% favouring the intervention" figure in the report. First, the counts are of *records*, and those records are overwhelmingly systematic reviews rather than primary studies. Reviews are not independent: they re-analyse heavily overlapping sets of the same trials, so a question reported as "1,026 of 1,095 records favour the intervention" rests on a far smaller body of primary evidence counted many times over. The near-zero corrected covered area seen on most questions does **not** establish independence — it is what a very large, varied pool of reviews produces mechanically, as pairwise-shared fractions are diluted by scale — and the low observed discordance is partly the same trials agreeing with themselves. Second, vote-counting by direction is an intentionally weak synthesis method: it ignores effect size, precision and sample size, treats a large meta-analysis and a single trial as one vote each, and is explicitly discouraged by Cochrane as a basis for conclusions. The percentages in this report are therefore best read as a coarse indicator of whether the literature leans one way, not as a measure of how much or how reliably.

**Publication bias and near-universal positivity.** On every effectiveness question the intervention is favoured in the high-80s to mid-90s per cent of records. That uniformity is itself a warning, not a reassurance: the depression-intervention literature is known to be affected by publication and reporting bias — positive trials are more likely to be published, and reviews of that literature inherit the skew — and a vote-count is maximally sensitive to exactly this bias. Because the review does not pool effects, it does not produce funnel plots or small-study-effect tests; the balance of registered-trial versus grey-literature evidence is therefore not formally assessed here. The consistent positivity across questions should be read as consistent with genuine benefit **and** with reporting bias, and the two cannot be separated on this evidence.

**Population and severity heterogeneity.** A further caution runs through every question: the records pool clinically different people. Baseline severity is, in the large majority of records, not stratified — mild, moderate and severe participants are combined — so an effect or a determinant is an average over the whole severity range rather than a value for a defined group. The populations themselves are also mixed: alongside general adult samples the corpus carries a substantial perinatal component (pregnant and postpartum women) and a tranche of pandemic-era studies, and it spans comorbid groups (for example people living with HIV) admitted under the common-mental-disorder scope. Effects and determinants reported here are therefore averaged across heterogeneous populations, which limits how precisely any figure applies to the specific group the ULCM will recruit, and is one reason directness would lower several confidence bands under full GRADE.

**Robustness.** Because a one-sided count is only informative if it survives the review's caveats, each intervention question also shows the share favouring the intervention within the subsets that matter: the higher-quality reviews, LMIC- and sub-Saharan-focused records, and non-specialist delivery. A signal that holds across these subsets is more dependable than one carried by the low-quality or high-income mass.

**Methodological quality.** The systematic reviews used as entry points are appraised with AMSTAR-2 (Shea et al. 2017) in a rapid critical-domains mode, collapsed to a confidence band of high, moderate, low or critically low. The band of a sourcing review is carried to the primary studies drawn from it; primary studies are not separately appraised.

**Overlap.** Where enough reviews report their pooled trial lists, the corrected covered area (CCA; Pieper et al. 2014) is reported. As noted above, a low CCA across a large review pool should be read as a scale artefact rather than as evidence of independence; it is included for transparency, not as a warrant that the counted evidence is separate.

**Confidence: GRADE-lite.** Each question carries a provisional GRADE-lite band. The full framework's five domains are review count and type, methodological quality, consistency of direction, directness, and precision. Given the three problems above — a predominantly low-quality review base, unverified extraction, and a vote-count that counts non-independent reviews and is insensitive to effect size and to publication bias — **confidence is capped at "Low" for every question in this report**. No question earns "Moderate" or "High"; questions with mixed or inconsistent direction, no high- or moderate-quality review, or a very small base are rated "Very low". This is deliberately conservative: it reflects that the report shows the *shape* of the evidence, not a verified estimate of its certainty, and directness and imprecision (particularly for sub-Saharan Africa) would lower several bands further under full GRADE. Two questions, the determinants mapping (RQ1) and the measurement-tools mapping (RQ18), are not effect questions; the harvest, vote-count and robustness tools are not applied to them, and they are presented descriptively.

## How to read a chapter

Every chapter opens with a metadata line (workstream, evidence stream, direction, GRADE-lite band), a key-message box, and the question. It then works through: the evidence base (with an AMSTAR-2 quality and geography figure); the direction and magnitude of effect (the harvest, and for several questions the same harvest stratified by geographic focus; for the dose, ingredients and group-size questions an unpooled distribution of standardized effect sizes); how robust the signal is across subsets; the question-specific detail (the dose profile, the components, the cost metrics, and so on); a note on cross-review overlap; a table of the strongest-contributing records; a set of representative extracted findings, each with its verbatim source; and a short answer box giving the bottom line, the confidence, and the implication for the model. The questions are directly comparable because they are assembled the same way. The complete, fully-columned extraction for each question is available in the accompanying `dex_by_rq.xlsx` workbook, one sheet per question.
